q: The net shear acting upward on the left of a section is:
n: By convention, net upward shear on the left of a section is positive shear. Source: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Gere & Goodno.

q: The net shear acting downward on the left of a section is:
n: Net downward shear on the left of a section is negative shear. Source: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis.

q: What is the tendency of a force to cause rotation, equal to force times moment arm?
n: Moment is the tendency of a force to cause rotation, equal to force × moment arm (M = F × d). Source: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics.

q: What is the sum of the moments on one side of a beam section?
n: The bending moment at a section is the sum of the moments of all forces on one side of it. Source: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis.

q: What slight upward curve is built into a beam to offset deflection?
n: Camber is a slight upward curve built into a beam to offset expected deflection. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What most often makes a slab on fill crack?
n: Slabs on fill most often crack from poorly compacted subgrade that later settles. Source: ACI 302.1R (Guide for Concrete Floor and Slab Construction).

q: Where is the main reinforcement in a cantilever slab?
n: A cantilever has negative moment, with tension on top, so the main bars go at the top. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: If a slab pour can't be finished in one go, where should it stop?
o: In the middle third of the span
n: Slab construction joints go in the middle third of the span, where shear is low. Source: ACI 301; NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.5.6.

q: When pouring concrete for beams and slabs, which should be poured first with a one-day interval?
o: It doesn't matter which is poured first
Both must be poured at the same time
n: Where beams and slabs cannot be cast monolithically, the beam is cast first and the slab later, about a day after, so the beam concrete can settle. Source: ACI 301; DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.

q: Which slab has no projections below its surface at all?
n: A flat plate has a uniform thickness with no projections below (no drop panels, capitals or beams). Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which slab carries heavy loads with no beams, using drop panels or capitals?
n: A flat slab carries heavy loads without beams, using drop panels or column capitals to resist punching shear. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which type of slab is easy to construct but more expensive due to its greater thickness?
n: Flat slabs are simple to form (no beams) but need greater thickness and concrete, so they cost more in materials. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which slab has closely spaced ribs in two directions for long spans and heavy loads?
n: A waffle (two-way joist) slab has closely spaced ribs in two directions, for long spans and heavy loads. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which slab is supported on two opposite sides only, suiting corridors?
n: A one-way slab, supported on two opposite sides, bends in one direction, which suits corridors. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: In a one-way slab, the main bars run:
o: Across the long span (parallel to the short span)
n: In a one-way slab the main bars span the short direction, between supports, at right angles to them. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4; Ching.

q: Which slab suits square or nearly square panels?
n: Two-way slabs suit square or nearly square panels, where the long-to-short span ratio is less than 2. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4 (two-way slabs).

q: What is the best location for drilling holes in a beam to minimize structural impact?
n: Holes in beams are best placed in the middle third of the span (around L/3 from supports), away from high-shear zones near supports. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; ACI guidance on web openings.

q: What is temperature reinforcement in a slab for?
o: Controlling cracks from temperature and shrinkage
n: Temperature (shrinkage) reinforcement controls cracking from shrinkage and temperature changes. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 424.4.

q: What lets a slab move with thermal expansion and contraction without cracking?
n: Expansion joints let a slab move with thermal expansion and contraction without cracking. Source: ACI 224.3R (Joints in Concrete Construction).

q: What horizontal member is mainly subject to bending?
n: A beam is a horizontal member mainly subject to bending. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: In a simply supported RC beam, which part is in tension?
n: Under positive moment, a simply supported RC beam has tension at the bottom, where the main bars go. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4.

q: What section property resists bending stress?
n: The section modulus (S = I/c) relates bending stress to moment, σ = M/S. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: What plate welded to a slender web prevents it from buckling?
n: A stiffener is a plate welded to a slender web to prevent it from buckling. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5 (Sec. 5G); AISC 360.

q: What is a beam or wall that rises above a slab and is cast with it?
n: An upstand (inverted) beam rises above the slab and is cast with it. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: While traversing EDSA, you can see the elevated MRT. What do you call the concrete portion running parallel to the road where the train tracks are placed?
n: The MRT-3 guideway is a precast concrete box girder carrying the tracks above EDSA. Source: DOTr MRT-3 project records; Ching.

q: What is a beam over more than two supports?
n: A continuous beam runs over more than two supports. Continuity over interior supports reduces midspan moments and deflection compared with a series of simple spans. Source: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis.

q: Which beam is thickened at its supports?
n: A haunched beam is thickened at its supports. The extra depth at the supports matches the larger negative moments and shears there. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What beam section appears as the letter "H" when vertical and the letter "I" when horizontal?
n: A wide-flange H-section reads as an "H" when its flanges are vertical and as an "I" when laid horizontally. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual; Ching.

q: Under positive bending, a beam is:
n: Under positive (sagging) bending, a beam is stretched below the neutral axis and compressed above it. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: Where does a simply supported beam see positive moment?
n: A simply supported beam has positive moment along its span, greatest at midspan under symmetric load. Source: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis.

q: Which bar is NOT normally found in a slab?
n: Slabs have bottom, top, temperature and distribution bars. Main vertical bars belong to walls and columns. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4.

q: What embedded length develops a bar's design strength at a critical section?
n: Development length (Ld) is the embedded length needed to develop a bar's design strength at a critical section. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 425.4.

q: Where does bending moment change sign along a beam?
n: Bending moment changes sign at the inflection point (point of contraflexure). Source: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis.
